The billable hour priced a dependence. The corporate client needed legal work it could not produce, and the firm sold the time it took to produce it. Clients are now hiring to end that dependence.

On October 11, Disney posted an opening for a Director of AI Enablement and Legal Engineering inside Legal and Global Affairs. The role designs AI systems for contract review, legal research, regulatory analysis and compliance, owns build-versus-buy decisions on legal technology and tracks the return on AI across the department. It requires a licensed attorney with at least ten years in practice. Disney is building the capacity to make legal work, and it wants a lawyer to judge it.

AT&T shows what that capacity does to the buying side. Its in-house legal agency, LegalEdge, launched in January and handled nearly 100 matters in its first six months. This month AT&T became an OpenAI design partner for legal workflows, and its general counsel has said its roster of about 30 national firms could shrink to 18 to 20 within two years.

The two sides read the moment differently. In Thomson Reuters' 2026 survey, 71 percent of in-house legal professionals expect outside firms to change their commercial models as AI spreads. Only 28 percent of law firms say they have made any change to their pricing in response.

Demand for outside counsel is not collapsing. More general counsel expect to raise outside spending than to cut it, 36 percent against 20, with M&A and regulatory work holding up. The composition is what moves. The work moving in-house is document review, legal research and first drafts, the base of the firm's pyramid. That base carried the leverage that pays partners and the apprenticeship that trains them. A firm that loses it loses revenue and its training ground in the same move.

Installing AI inside the firm does not close the gap. If the tools cut the hours and the firm still sells hours, it has made its own product cheaper and kept the pricing model that its clients are leaving. The question has moved from whether a firm uses AI to what the firm sells once its client uses AI too: judgment, accountability and the outcome of matters that cannot come home.

A firm can choose the pace of its own transformation. It cannot choose how long its clients will wait.

When I suggest someone takes advantage of my Free CV Check, I sometimes hear reasons why they don't need one.

I understand, but here's why I'd challenge four of them.

"I've already had my CV professionally reviewed."

Fair enough. But by whom?

There are some excellent CV writers out there, but not everyone offering reviews has the experience or industry knowledge you'd expect.

I've seen CVs people have paid to have professionally reviewed where I've immediately spotted what I consider fundamental problems.

"Recruiters have told me my CV is good."

That's encouraging. But how many recruiters?

Consistently positive feedback from recruiters and hiring managers over the years is reassuring. But one or two opinions don't necessarily mean your CV couldn't be improved.

My nan would've told me my CV was brilliant too!

"My CV has always got me jobs in the past."

Great. But what about the roles you didn't get?

The applications that went nowhere? The recruiters who never got back to you?
You'll never know how many opportunities you may have missed because your CV didn't make the right impression.

And the market and recruitment methods have changed, including increased use of automation and AI. What worked years ago might not be as effective today.

"I'm too busy applying for roles."

If you're applying for dozens of roles without getting interviews, surely it's worth checking whether your CV might be part of the problem?

You could send another 50 applications with the same CV, or improve it first and then carry on. I'd choose the second option.

And make sure your LinkedIn profile is up to scratch too. Both matter.

So why do I offer a Free CV Check?

I'm not a professional CV writer, and I've never claimed to be one.

But I've worked in IT for over 30 years, spent 28+ years contracting and reviewed more than 4,800 CVs.

My Free CV Check is exactly that. Free.

I'll tell you the ONE thing I'd improve first. If it's already in great shape, I'll tell you that too.

There's absolutely no obligation to buy anything from me. I want to help you give yourself the best possible chance of securing your next role.

And if you've already had one and made the suggested changes, just email your updated CV back to me for a free re-check!

You paid for the software. But do you own everything needed to run it?
This is an important question businesses should resolve before signing a development contract—not after launch.
When hiring a software development agency, clarify ownership and access across five areas:
1. Source code
Who owns the intellectual property, and will you receive repository access and the necessary documentation?
2. Design assets
Will editable design files, brand assets, and relevant project files be handed over?
3. Domain ownership
Is the domain registered under your business's account, with you retaining administrative control?
4. Hosting and deployment
Who controls the cloud provider, server, production environment, and deployment pipeline?
5. Third-party dependencies
Are any libraries, templates, fonts, plugins, or services governed by separate licenses or recurring fees?
A professional handover should also address credentials, backups, documentation, security, and ongoing maintenance.
One important distinction: access, legal ownership, and intellectual property rights are not the same thing. Contracts should specify what transfers to the client, when it transfers, and what remains subject to third-party licenses.
At AI Dev Planner, we believe clients should understand these arrangements before development begins.

The question I get asked most is how we’re finding the market. I thought I’d share what we’re seeing and a few things I’ve been thinking about. I’d love to hear your take, too.

So far, our work has been steady. That’s likely partly because we focus on mid- and senior-level roles, especially in technology, where clients need help finding specialized talent. We’re seeing demand for AI and machine learning engineers, data engineers, forward-deployed engineers and automation specialists. We also do a lot of project and contract work, which tends to pick up during uncertain times as companies hesitate to commit to permanent hires. Our global staffing business has also been busy.

My concern right now is more about people trying to get their first job.

Indeed’s Canadian research found that in February 2025, postings for standard and junior tech roles were 25% below February 2020 levels, while senior and management postings were 5% above. 

We can’t say AI caused that decline. But if companies automate more of the tasks we used to give junior employees, where will they get the experience to become the people we need later? Those assignments may seem routine to someone experienced, but they’re often how you learn to think through a problem and develop judgment.

Of course, I’m also concerned about what happens further down the road as the models get better. Businesses understandably want to become more efficient, but if that means fewer people earning a good living, there are consequences for businesses too. People need income to buy what we’re selling. The effects reach beyond the people who lose their jobs. This becomes a societal problem that all of us have a stake in addressing.

I’m not convinced income support alone is the answer. Financial security matters, of course, but work means more to people than a paycheque. It can provide purpose, relationships and a sense of contributing.

I read an article about Bill Gates’s proposal to tax robots to discourage businesses from replacing people with machines. His argument is that employers pay payroll taxes when they hire people, while buying a robot can come with a tax write-off. He wants to reduce that incentive to replace people and use the revenue to fund retraining and support affected workers. I think that’s worth discussing. It also makes me wonder whether we should look at reducing the taxes attached to employing people.

I don’t have a settled view on the policy. But I do think businesses need to consider how people will get their start and build experience as the work changes.

I’d really like to hear how others are thinking about this.

🚨 AI Agents don't just need better prompts. They need CONTRACTS.
We spend a lot of time improving:
🧠 Reasoning
📝 Prompts
🔧 Tool Calling
💾 Memory
🤖 Multi-Agent Orchestration
But production systems eventually hit a different problem:
What exactly is each agent allowed—and expected—to do?
If Agent A sends something to Agent B, hoping they'll “figure it out,” we've created another distributed system with an undocumented API. 😅
Production Agentic AI needs explicit Agent Contracts:
✅ Input / Output Schemas
✅ Structured Responses
✅ Tool Permissions
✅ Authentication & Authorization
✅ Timeout & Retry Policies
✅ Confidence Thresholds
✅ Error Handling
✅ State Transitions
✅ Human Escalation Rules
✅ Audit & Traceability
Instead of:
Agent A → “Research this” → Agent B
Think:
Agent A → Typed Task → Validated Output → Agent B
And if the contract is violated?
Fail predictably. Don't improvise silently.
As AI systems become more distributed, agent communication starts looking surprisingly familiar:
APIs + Events + State Machines + Policies + Observability
The future of Agentic AI won't only be about smarter agents.
It will be about well-engineered systems of agents.

What's MOST important in an Agent Contract?
A) Structured Input / Output
B) Permissions & Security
C) Failure / Retry Behavior

THE CAPITAL BRIEF | ISSUE 04

$7 TRILLION LATER, AI HAS A CREDIT QUESTION.

Can the cash flow carry the debt?

For most of the AI boom, investors have been asking an equity question:

How big can this become?

Credit markets are beginning to ask a very different one:

Who gets repaid?

S&P Global estimates that six of the world’s largest hyperscalers could spend more than $7 trillion on AI-related capital expenditure between 2025 and 2030.

But the financing underneath that buildout is becoming impossible to ignore.

CoreWeave bonds issued earlier this year at a 9.675% yield recently moved toward 15% as investors demanded significantly more compensation for the risk.

Meanwhile, AI infrastructure financing continues.

Today, Nebius announced a new $3.5 billion financing facility from Citi to support data-centre expansion and GPU purchases.

This does not mean the AI thesis is broken.

It means the conversation is changing.

For an equity investor, the question may be:

How quickly can revenue grow?

For a lender, the questions are different:

Who is actually signing the customer contracts?

How predictable is the cash flow?

How much leverage sits ahead of us?

What happens if today’s GPUs become tomorrow’s outdated equipment?

Revenue visibility, leverage, technology obsolescence, or power availability?

Europe is short 502,000 truck drivers. And the gap is getting wider, not narrower.

Let me frame this differently than most industry commentary does.

This isn't a hiring problem. It's a structural failure of an entire labor model — and the companies that understand this distinction are already building something different.

The numbers from the International Road Transport Union are brutal: a 13% shortage rate across Europe. Two-thirds of road transport operators are actively turning down contracts because they literally cannot staff the trucks. And here's the kicker — roughly 660,000 current European truck drivers will hit retirement age by 2030. That's 20% of the entire workforce disappearing in less than four years.

Wage increases? Already happening. Working condition improvements? Underway. Digital scheduling flexibility, modern fleet investments, lifestyle marketing to younger demographics? All being tried.

And none of it is closing the gap fast enough.

Which is why September 2026 might be remembered as a turning point.

Einride and Lidl just deployed the first cab-less SAE Level 4 autonomous truck in daily commercial operations on a public road in Germany. Not a pilot. Not a demo. A real truck, carrying real goods, on a real road, on a regular schedule — with no driver and no safety operator on board.

The German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) granted the permit. If you know anything about German road safety standards, you know this isn't a rubber stamp.

And this isn't Einride's first rodeo. They've been running driverless heavy-duty operations across Sweden, Norway, and Belgium for months. The DAF Trucks partnership (backed by PACCAR) is preparing factory-ready Level 4 electric trucks for scaled deployment. NVIDIA's Hyperion platform and Alpamayo AI reasoning model are being integrated to handle increasingly complex environments.

But here's what the tech headlines miss — and what matters for freight forwarders like us:

𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝗸𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗱𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗱𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘀𝘁.

The strategy emerging across Northern and Western Europe is surgical:

→ Autonomous trucks handle the boring, repetitive, high-capacity motorway corridors (hub-to-hub). The routes nobody wants to drive. The night shifts that destroy retention rates.

→ Human drivers handle the work that actually requires human judgment — complex terminal operations, border crossings, urban last-mile delivery, and customer-facing interactions.

→ Predictive analytics and automated workflow tools reduce the administrative burden on existing drivers, making the profession more attractive to younger workers who expect digital-first workplaces.

This isn't about replacing people. It's about finally building a system that doesn't collapse when you can't find enough people to fill it.

At Fortuna Nord, we're watching this transition closely — not as spectators, but as active participants. Our Nordic corridor operations already integrate with the most advanced fleet technologies in Scandinavia, and we're positioning our network for the hybrid human-autonomous model that will define European road freight by 2030.

The driver shortage isn't a temporary crisis. It's the permanent new reality. The only question is whether your logistics infrastructure is designed for the workforce that exists — or the one you wish you had.

We need to talk about application volume and the dangerous AI "doom loop" breaking recruitment.

Greenhouse Software 2026 recruiting benchmarks show that average applications per job increased from 116 in 2022 to 244 in 2025. That is a 111% explosion in volume in just three years.

But here is the question hiring leaders should be asking: Did the talent pool actually become twice as strong, or did the volume of applications simply inflate?

The data tells a stark story. The surge isn't because talent multiplied; it's because candidates are making use of  AI. Job seekers are spending a few dollars on auto-apply bots that fire off hundreds of applications a week with minimal effort, alongside generative tools that polish CVs into a "sea of sameness."
As a result, annual applications per recruiter surged from 1,610 in 2022 to 4,890 in 2025. That is a 412% increase in administrative noise impacting TA teams that have simultaneously been cut by over 50%.
This has triggered an AI arms race:
- On the candidate side: AI is used to blast applications.
- On the hiring side: AI screening tools are deployed to aggressively filter out the noise.
So who should be complaining?

Job seekers/Applicants are terrified of disappearing into automated corporate black holes. Meanwhile, companies are drowning in profiles but starving for true capability. In most recent times there's been a calling out on both sides, each side leaning more into an interesting perspective where only outcomes rely on personal rewards, but realistically regulating personal AI use is an impossible, tasking uphill battle.

The real divide lies in where both sides put in the work.

My view on AI hiring: AI can easily manage volume, but it cannot compensate for a poorly defined role or a weak assessment process. The true advantage will not belong to the company processing the most CVs via an algorithm. It will belong to the organization that can reliably identify human capability proactively.

AI can match keywords, but as of now, it fails miserably at detecting emotional intelligence, reading unwritten career trajectories, or assessing cultural resonance. A machine cannot feel the spark of human potential or test for soft skill adaptability in a dynamic environment.
The primary challenge today isn't finding candidates. AI has made that too easy. Same CV/Profiles, Same responses. The problem is identifying the right ones.

Let’s get the discussion going:
 - Is this AI battle creating more efficiency, or is it breaking the social contract of hiring? Who is losing/winning more in this paradox...the candidate/job applicants or with hiring teams?

I'm excited about AI agents. I really am.

The idea that software can actually get things done for us, instead of just answering questions, is pretty incredible.

But how much freedom are we comfortable giving it?

Imagine an AI agent handling customer support. It reads an email, checks the customer's account, updates the CRM, and sends a response. 

All without anyone getting involved. Great, right?

Until it offers a refund it wasn't authorized to give. Or changes the wrong customer's information. Or sends something it really shouldn't have. 🤯 

And suddenly, that convenient little workflow becomes a much bigger problem.

What interests me is where we draw the line. 

I'm perfectly happy letting an agent organize my inbox, summarize documents, or schedule meetings.

But would I let one negotiate a contract on my behalf? Move money? Make a hiring decision? Send a sensitive email without me seeing it first?

Probably not. At least not today.

And I wonder how much of this will change as agents get better.

Will we gradually become comfortable giving them more control? 
Will we even notice when that happens?

We're already getting used to AI making recommendations. The next step is getting used to AI acting on them.

And that's a pretty significant difference.

As someone building in AI safety, I want agents to become more capable. I also want us to be a lot more thoughtful about what we're actually giving them permission to do.

Especially when their actions affect other people. I'm curious where everyone else stands on this.

What's something you'd happily let an AI agent do for you, and what's one thing you absolutely wouldn't?

Marketplaces are not only matching engines. They are uncertainty-reduction systems.

A marketplace helps people evaluate unfamiliar providers and manage a transaction. Matching is only the first part. Buyers also need identity, relevant history, visible proof and a clear delivery process. Payment and review arrangements add another layer of information. Considering the full stack makes it easier to see where uncertainty still exists.

Finding a provider answers who might help. Understanding their scope, delivery process and payment workflow answers how the work will happen. A dependable transaction needs both kinds of information instead of assuming discovery completes the decision.

1. Inspect who the creator is and what they have done.
2. Connect proof to the work you need.
3. Understand the proposed project structure.
4. Clarify communication, review and payment expectations.

Use platform information together with thoughtful project questions. No single signal explains whether an offer fits every buyer and every assignment.

Founders. Nobody understands what you’re going through except… every other founder. 

Building an ocean company is a strange kind of lonely. Your sales cycles are measured in years. Your hardware has to survive salt water. Your investors mostly come from software. And the few people who truly understand are scattered across Oslo, Singapore, Boston and Marseille.

I see it every week. Brilliant founders hit the same walls in the same order: de-risking R&D, landing the first industrial contract, hiring a VP Sales, raising an A or a B when the market wants AI multiples.

Same walls. Different companies. No one comparing notes.

That’s why we’re launching Ocean Scalers: small circles of ocean CEOs at the same stage, who don’t compete with each other, meeting every quarter for a year with an experienced facilitator. CEOs only. Open to every ocean CEO, not only the Rypples portfolio.

This isn’t networking. It’s the room where you say what you can’t say to your board, your team or your investors. Then you get honest answers from people who’ve hit the same wall. 

The ocean doesn’t need more prototypes. It needs more companies that scale. Scaling is learned faster together. First circles start in January. 

Applications close 20 November. Link in comments.

Some recruitment organisations really are pretty sh1t with their standards, processes and service.  

I’m not talking Ai or automation or anything overly funky or groundbreaking.  That has its place, for sure. 

I’m not talking revolutionary ‘blue skies thinking’ and market leading serivice lines. They too have their place.  

I’m talking companies that can’t even be arsed to do the absolute basics…. 

- do you reference the candidates to place on behalf of a customer.  To validate capability, but more importantly to speak to a hiring manager in your space.  Who hired this person?  Is it tracked & reported via the CRM. 

- do you meet all your placed candidates and active buying clients regularly to build true relationships?  Is it tracked & reported viw the CRM. 

- do you have a process to regularly monitor the performance of all your contractors you are supplying.  Is it tracked on the CRM and reported. 

- do you always look to backfill every resignation you create by filling a job.  Is it tracked and reported on the CRM.  

- do you even understand how many new contract placements you can make by tracking end dates & people movement.  Is it tracked and built on the CRM. 

- do you track every contractor that finishes for you to their next project? Every time.  Is it on the CRM and reported? 

- do you understand what lifetime value of a candidate (perm or contract) is?  If you don’t understand lifetime value you’re losing bags of cash. 💰 


There’s hundreds of simple processes 👆that executed on every desk, consistently and with quality leads to regular client wins and more placements.  I don’t mean sometimes we do some of this on some desks.  I mean it’s your DNA and it’s lived and breathed.  Without exception.   It’s a standard you own as the leader.  You demand it because it’s your strategy. 

And yes lots of the above can be automated now.  That’s another discussion.  

I’m talking basic stuff thats died and just doesn’t seem to happen anymore.  Lazy? Incompetent?  Can’t be arsed?  Sh1t leadership?  Loose standards?  Too many exceptions to keep average people happy doing what they’ve always done?  Just turn up and accept mediocre performance? Blind to how to actually do it all?  Don’t use your CRM?  

Sharpen up on the basics before you get carried away with Ai and intergalactic strategies.   Lots of performance and sales opportunities are sitting under your nose if you’re prepared to look. 

Over & out.

I wanted to know what UAE start-ups are actually buying when they acquire other companies.

announcements usually say similar things like "accelerated growth" or "strategic synergies", but these tell you remarkably little about what anyone actually bought.

yet, 3 acquisitions in the last year really caught my attention.

first, Ray powerbank sharing.

Installing a powerbank station into a restaurant or hotel or shopping mall is an extremely long and resource intensive process. So in May, Ray acquired the operating assets of its competitor JetCharge, including its hardware, team and contracts covering 100+ locations.

Then take CNTXT AI - the abu dhabi AI company.

in June, it acquired Actualize which specialises in arabic voice AI, including models adapted to regional dialects. What interested me was not necessarily the tech part, it was how CNTXT integrated Actualize's key personnel. Its co founders joined CNTXT as CTO and VP of AI.

And then PopArabia - the music company with capabilities across music publishing, licensing and right managment. 

It acquired Viral Wave - a music distribution business in April. It gave Pop Arabia infrastructure, expertise and relationship to distribute and monetise music across streaming platforms and Youtube.

So - 3 very different companies that all bought 3 very different things:
Ray bought ACCESS
CNTXT AI bought TECHNICAL CAPABILITY
PopArabia bought DISTRIBUTION

none of these things are particularly easy to recreate simply by hiring more people. 

which makes me think about the number of conversations I've had with founders about what they should build next, which capabilities to hire for, or how to accelerate growth.

there is perhaps another question worth asking... 

What would take us 2 years to build, that someone else has already spent 5+ years getting right?

now of course, buying something is much simpler than integrating it. But I think there is a lot of value in Time, Relationships and Mistakes - that you no longer have to accumulate yourself.

🤖 Greater use of technology, including AI

🔹 The UK was among the countries reporting increased manufacturing employment

✅ Growing workloads don’t always lead to permanent headcount
✅ Some clients will go permanent, others temp or contract, and some will try to do more with the same team
✅ The strongest opportunities come from understanding which route each client is taking

Kumo HR — 1153. HRTech Solution

Most HR teams don't have an automation problem. They have an execution problem.
The tools are already there. An ATS here, a payroll engine there, a leave calendar somewhere else. What's missing is the person in the middle: the one who opens each system, pulls the data, spots the conflict, drafts the document and chases the approval. That work never shows up on a feature list, but it eats the week. And the current wave of "AI assistants" hasn't touched it — a copilot that suggests a next step still leaves the step to you.

Kumo HR is built exactly at that point.

Kumo positions itself not as a chatbot layer but as an agentic operating system for HR. Its Agent 2.0 takes a goal in plain language — build a hiring plan, audit our leave this week, run a 360 for engineering — breaks it into a mission, executes each step, and reads what each tool actually returned before deciding what comes next. It parses CVs, contracts and policies rather than just summarising them, and it produces artifacts: hiring plans, job posts, audits, reports, all versioned and reusable.

The control architecture is where it gets interesting for anyone who has been burned by automation. Sensitive actions are confirm-gated — the agent drafts and stops. Every step, tool call and result is logged. Teams can define Skills, so a process taught once runs the same way for everyone afterward.

Underneath sits a full HR platform: people and org, hiring, multi-entity payroll and expenses, performance and 360, leave and time, learning, engagement, documents and e-signature. Employer-of-Record coverage extends to 180+ countries with localised contracts and regulatory tracking. For technical teams, Kumo exposes an Agent API, an MCP server and a TypeScript SDK, so the agent can be embedded into another product or connected to systems already in use.

An independent note. The agentic comparison Kumo publishes — copilot versus agent — is its own qualitative assessment, not a third-party benchmark, and the company says so openly. That transparency is welcome, but it shifts the burden to the buyer: the only meaningful test is running a real mission on your own data and reading the log line by line. Two questions worth asking in a demo. First: when the agent hits an ambiguous case, what exactly does it do — stop, guess, or escalate? Second, for teams operating in Türkiye: local payroll and social security compliance is not on the published country logic, so where does that boundary sit?

This was during a seasonal hiring ramp for Amazon India, when I was running the contract-staffing business at Aasaanjobs / OLX People.

Recruiting thousands of people was one challenge. Making sure the operations could handle that scale was another.

Every person needed to be onboarded, their identity and bank details verified, their salary calculated and paid correctly, and statutory compliance managed. With seasonal hiring came significant attrition, which meant processing exits and full and final settlements alongside thousands of new joiners.

And unlike recruitment, much of this work had to happen again every month.

The only way our systems could keep up was through automation. Our team had built technology to automate onboarding documents, identity and bank-account verification, payroll calculations, compliance processes and much of the repetitive administration across the contract-staffing + Employer-of-Record business.

This allowed our operations team to focus on exceptions and problems that actually needed human intervention, rather than manually processing the same checks for tens of thousands of people.

We were doing this well before today's AI tools became available. But the underlying principle is the same reason I find AI so useful now: automate the repetitive work and give people more time for decisions that need their attention.

One thing that experience taught me is that scaling a business requires much more than increasing headcount or winning new contracts. Your people, processes, technology, compliance, financial controls and operational capacity all need to scale together.
